advances: Proves the uniform planar slice bound with \(\delta=1/76\). For every primitive three-dimensional sheared polygon prism in the subgoal, it gives an original height of mass at least \(W/152\) and an original center at that height whose true original-weight singleton-band halfspace depth is at least \(W/304=(1/38)W/2^3\). Thus this entire prism family satisfies the bounded-band conclusion already with band width zero. This does not resolve the higher-dimensional rank-one selection problem or the locked weak Oertel conjecture.

proof:
The planar support \(A\) is finite and nonempty. Let \(w_{\max}=\max_{p\in A}w_p\) and \(M_*=\max_{s\in\mathbb Z}M_s\), both positive. For each occupied integer height \(s\), select one point \(p_s=(s,z_s)\in A\) of maximum weight at that height, and put \(U=\sum_{s:M_s>0}w_{p_s}\). We first prove \(U\le12w_{\max}\), without any bound on \(\beta\).

For every original point \(p=(s,z)\in A\), set \(\phi_p=\log(w_{\max}/w_p)\ge0\). If \(p=(s,z)\) and \(p'=(s',z')\) have the same coordinatewise parity, their midpoint is an integer point of \(R\), hence belongs to the complete support \(A\). Direct expansion gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_{(p+p')/2}
&=\frac{\phi_p+\phi_{p'}}2-\frac{(s-s')^2}{4},\\
\phi_p,\phi_{p'}\le v
&\ \Longrightarrow\quad
0\le\phi_{(p+p')/2}\le v-\frac{(s-s')^2}{4}
\qquad(v\ge0).
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently, within each of the four parity classes, the selected points \(p_s\) with \(\phi_{p_s}\le v\) have height diameter at most \(2\sqrt v\). The selected heights are distinct integers. Each class therefore contains at most \(\lfloor2\sqrt v\rfloor+1\) such points. The midpoint need not be a selected point: its nonnegative potential follows from the maximum over the full original support. Summing the elementary identity \(e^{-a}=\int_a^\infty e^{-v}\,dv\) for the finitely many selected potentials, and using \(2\sqrt v\le v+1\), yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{U}{w_{\max}}
&=\int_0^\infty e^{-v}
\bigl|\{s:M_s>0,\ \phi_{p_s}\le v\}\bigr|\,dv\\
&\le4\int_0^\infty e^{-v}(2\sqrt v+1)\,dv\\
&\le4\int_0^\infty e^{-v}(v+2)\,dv=12.
\end{aligned}
\]

Every occupied vertical section of the convex polygon is a closed real interval, and its lattice points are a finite consecutive integer interval. If \(\beta\ge\log2\), its maximum-weight point is its largest integer \(z\), and summing backward from that point gives \(M_s\le w_{p_s}/(1-e^{-\beta})\le2w_{p_s}\). If \(\beta\le-\log2\), summing forward from the smallest integer \(z\) gives the same bound. Thus \(|\beta|\ge\log2\) implies \(W\le2U\le24w_{\max}\le24M_*\).

Now assume \(|\beta|\le\log2\). Let \(E\subset\mathbb R\) be the projection of \(R\) onto its first coordinate. It is a compact interval. For \(s\in E\), write the nonempty real section as \(\{z:(s,z)\in R\}=[a(s),b(s)]\) and put \(\ell(s)=b(s)-a(s)\). Convexity of \(R\), applied to the lower and upper endpoints of two sections, proves that \(a\) is convex and \(b\) is concave on \(E\). Hence \(\ell\) is concave. The set \(\mathcal I=\{s\in E:\ell(s)\ge1\}\) is an interval, possibly empty or a singleton. It is closed: if \(s_i\in\mathcal I\) tends to \(s\), compactness of \(R\) gives a subsequence of pairs of section endpoints tending to two points of the section at \(s\) whose \(z\)-coordinates differ by at least one. That section has length at least one. Thus \(\mathcal I\) is compact.

An occupied integer height outside \(\mathcal I\) has section length less than one, so it contains at most one lattice point. This includes all length-zero sections. Its mass is therefore its selected maximum weight. It follows that \(\sum_{s\in\mathbb Z:s\notin\mathcal I}M_s\le U\le12M_*\). Heights in \(\mathcal I\cap\mathbb Z\) will be called wide heights. A closed interval of length at least one always contains an integer, so every wide height is occupied.

We next compare the discrete mass of a wide row to its continuous integral, including arbitrary fractional endpoints. Fix real \(a\le b\) with \(b-a\ge1\), put \(B=[a,b]\cap\mathbb Z\), and for \(j\in B\) let \(E_j=[j-1,j+1]\cap[a,b]\). Each \(E_j\) has length between one and two. Indeed its length is \(\min(1,j-a)+\min(1,b-j)\), which is at least one because \(j-a,b-j\ge0\) and their sum is at least one.

The intervals \(E_j\) cover \([a,b]\). Between the first and last integers of \(B\), one may choose an adjacent integer; between \(a\) and the first integer, or between the last integer and \(b\), the corresponding endpoint integer has distance less than one. At almost every real point, at most two of the intervals \(E_j\) overlap, because \(E_j\subseteq[j-1,j+1]\) and the indices \(j\) are distinct integers. The possible threefold overlaps occur only at integers and have Lebesgue measure zero. Moreover, whenever \(z\in E_j\), the tilt bound gives \(\frac12e^{\beta j}\le e^{\beta z}\le2e^{\beta j}\). Consequently,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac12\sum_{j\in B}e^{\beta j}
&\le\sum_{j\in B}\int_{E_j}e^{\beta z}\,dz
\le2\int_a^b e^{\beta z}\,dz,\\
\int_a^b e^{\beta z}\,dz
&\le\sum_{j\in B}\int_{E_j}e^{\beta z}\,dz
\le4\sum_{j\in B}e^{\beta j}.
\end{aligned}
\]

In particular the integral and the discrete sum compare in both directions by a factor of four. Integer endpoints of \([a,b]\) are included in \(B\); no boundary atom has been discarded.

If \(\mathcal I\cap\mathbb Z\) is empty, the bound \(W\le12M_*\) already proves the planar assertion. Otherwise define, for every real \(s\in\mathcal I\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
G(s)&=\int_{a(s)}^{b(s)}e^{\beta z}\,dz,\\
F(s)&=\exp\bigl(-(s-h)^2+\alpha s\bigr)G(s).
\end{aligned}
\]

These functions are positive because \(\ell(s)\ge1\). The preceding comparison gives \(F(s)/4\le M_s\le4F(s)\) for every \(s\in\mathcal I\cap\mathbb Z\).

The function \(\log G\) is concave on \(\mathcal I\). This follows directly from the formulas

\[
\log G(s)=
\begin{cases}
\beta b(s)+\log\bigl(1-e^{-\beta\ell(s)}\bigr)-\log\beta,
&\beta>0,\\
\beta a(s)+\log\bigl(1-e^{\beta\ell(s)}\bigr)-\log(-\beta),
&\beta<0,\\
\log\ell(s),&\beta=0.
\end{cases}
\]

For \(c>0\), the function \(r\mapsto\log(1-e^{-cr})\) on \(r>0\) is increasing and concave: its first derivative is \(c/(e^{cr}-1)>0\) and its second derivative is \(-c^2e^{cr}/(e^{cr}-1)^2<0\). Its composition with the positive concave function \(\ell\) is concave. Also \(\beta b\) is concave when \(\beta>0\), and \(\beta a\) is concave when \(\beta<0\). The case \(\beta=0\) follows because the logarithm is increasing and concave. All these formulas remain valid at the endpoints of \(\mathcal I\), since \(\ell\ge1\) there.

It follows that \(s\mapsto\log F(s)+s^2=(2h+\alpha)s-h^2+\log G(s)\) is concave on \(\mathcal I\). The integers in the compact interval \(\mathcal I\) form a finite consecutive interval. Choose a maximizing integer \(m\in\mathcal I\cap\mathbb Z\) for \(F\) on that set. Whenever \(k-1,k,k+1\) belong to that set, midpoint concavity gives

\[
\log F(k+1)-2\log F(k)+\log F(k-1)\le-2.
\]

On the right of \(m\), if a first neighbor exists, the first increment \(\log F(m+1)-\log F(m)\) is nonpositive. Each subsequent increment is at most the previous one minus two. Summing the first \(j\) increments therefore gives \(\log F(m+j)-\log F(m)\le-j(j-1)\). The identical argument applied in the reverse order gives the same bound at \(m-j\). The consecutive-interval property ensures that every intervening neighbor exists whenever the indicated outer point exists. Thus this argument also applies when \(m\) is a truncated endpoint or when there is a tie for the maximum. We obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s\in\mathcal I\cap\mathbb Z}F(s)
&\le F(m)\left(1+2\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}e^{-j(j-1)}\right)\\
&=F(m)\left(3+2\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}e^{-j(j-1)}\right)\\
&\le F(m)\left(3+\frac{2}{e^2-1}\right)
<4F(m).
\end{aligned}
\]

For the last two steps, \(j(j-1)\ge2(j-1)\) for \(j\ge2\), and \(e>2\). The estimate also holds if the integer interval consists only of \(m\). Combining it with both row-integral comparisons proves

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s\in\mathcal I\cap\mathbb Z}M_s
&\le4\sum_{s\in\mathcal I\cap\mathbb Z}F(s)
\le16F(m)\le64M_m\le64M_*,\\
W&\le12M_*+64M_*=76M_*.
\end{aligned}
\]

Together with the large-tilt case, this proves the planar bound for all the stated parameters.

We now prove the prism assertion, retaining the original support and original weights. Coprimality gives integers \(\rho,\sigma\) with \(L\sigma-M\rho=1\). The planar chart

\[
\begin{aligned}
s&=Lx+My,&z&=\rho x+\sigma y,\\
x&=\sigma s-Mz,&y&=-\rho s+Lz
\end{aligned}
\]

is unimodular: both the chart and its displayed inverse have integer coefficients, and its determinant is one. Let \(R\) be the image of \(Q\) under this chart. It is a compact full-dimensional convex polygon, and its complete lattice support is exactly the image of \(Q\cap\mathbb Z^2\). This follows in both directions from the integer chart and integer inverse.

Add \(u=t-Lx-My=t-s\). The map \((x,y,t)\mapsto(s,z,u)\) has inverse \((s,z,u)\mapsto(\sigma s-Mz,-\rho s+Lz,s+u)\). Both maps have integer coefficients and determinant one, and the map takes \(P\) exactly to \(R\times[0,1]\). In particular \(P\) is a compact full-dimensional convex body. Its full lattice support is in bijection with \((R\cap\mathbb Z^2)\times\{0,1\}\). Equivalently, in original coordinates it is exactly

\[
D=\{(x,y,Lx+My+u):(x,y)\in Q\cap\mathbb Z^2,\ u\in\{0,1\}\}.
\]

The two displayed residual values are the only possible integers in the closed interval \([0,1]\), and both occur over every original base point. Thus there is no lattice index factor and no omitted boundary row.

Set \(\alpha'=\alpha\sigma-\beta\rho\) and \(\beta'=\beta L-\alpha M\). In these coordinates the original weight, for either \(u\in\{0,1\}\), is exactly

\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{(\sigma s-Mz,-\rho s+Lz,s+u)}
&=\exp\bigl(-((s+u)-h)^2+\alpha's+\beta'z\bigr)\\
&=\exp\bigl(-(s-(h-u))^2+\alpha's+\beta'z\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the residual level \(u\), with its entire complete planar support, is an instance of the proved planar assertion with Gaussian center \(h-u\) and affine coefficients \(\alpha',\beta'\).

For clarity, index each residual row by its original height \(k\), and set

\[
\begin{aligned}
W_{k,u}
&=\exp\bigl(-(k-h)^2\bigr)
\sum_{\substack{(x,y)\in Q\cap\mathbb Z^2\\Lx+My=k-u}}
\exp(\alpha x+\beta y),\\
W^{(u)}&=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}W_{k,u}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The exact alias between planar and original row indices is that the planar row at chart height \(s\) in residual level \(u\) has mass \(W_{s+u,u}\). Moreover \(W_k=W_{k,0}+W_{k,1}\) and \(W=W^{(0)}+W^{(1)}\). Applying the planar assertion separately to the two complete residual levels gives \(\max_k W_{k,u}\ge W^{(u)}/76\) for each \(u\). Choose \(u_0\in\{0,1\}\) with \(W^{(u_0)}\ge W/2\), and choose \(k_0\) attaining the maximum row mass in that level. Then \(W_{k_0,u_0}\ge W/152\), and consequently \(W_{k_0}\ge W/152\).

It remains to certify actual ambient depth at a single original center. In the row just chosen, the chart value \(s=k_0-u_0\) is fixed, and all original points have the form

\[
(\sigma(k_0-u_0)-Mz,\ -\rho(k_0-u_0)+Lz,\ k_0)
\qquad
(z\in\mathbb Z,\ (k_0-u_0,z)\in R).
\]

They lie on one affine line of direction \((-M,L,0)\). The allowable \(z\)'s form a finite nonempty consecutive integer interval, because \(R\) is convex and the support is complete. All their original weights are positive. Choose the first \(z_0\) in increasing order whose cumulative weight reaches at least half of \(W_{k_0,u_0}\), and let \(J\) be its displayed original point. The row mass with \(z\le z_0\) is at least \(W_{k_0,u_0}/2\). The mass with \(z<z_0\) is strictly less than that half, so the mass with \(z\ge z_0\) is also at least \(W_{k_0,u_0}/2\). These statements include the median atom in both closed halflines.

Every ambient closed halfspace \(H\subseteq\mathbb R^3\) containing \(J\) restricts on this affine line either to the whole line or to a closed halfline containing \(z_0\). This follows by substituting the affine parametrization into its defining linear inequality; if the coefficient of \(z\) is zero, containment of \(J\) makes the whole line satisfy it. Otherwise the resulting containing halfline includes either all \(z\le z_0\) or all \(z\ge z_0\). Hence \(H\) contains at least half of the chosen row's original weight. The complete singleton height band also contains the other residual row at height \(k_0\), whose weights are nonnegative, so

\[
\sum_{\substack{I\in D\cap H\\I_3=k_0}}w_I
\ge\frac12W_{k_0,u_0}
\ge\frac{W}{304}
\qquad
(H\text{ any closed halfspace with }J\in H).
\]

Taking the infimum over these halfspaces proves \(\tau_{[k_0,k_0]}(J)\ge W/304\). The selected \(J\) is an original lattice point, and the interval \([k_0,k_0]\) is a permitted closed singleton band of width zero. This proves all the prism conclusions.
statement:
Let \(R\subset\mathbb R^2\) be any compact full-dimensional convex polygon, with nonempty complete lattice support \(A=R\cap\mathbb Z^2\). For arbitrary \(h,\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\), define

\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{(s,z)}&=\exp\bigl(-(s-h)^2+\alpha s+\beta z\bigr)
&&((s,z)\in A),\\
M_s&=\sum_{\substack{z\in\mathbb Z\\(s,z)\in A}}w_{(s,z)}
&&(s\in\mathbb Z),\\
W&=\sum_{s\in\mathbb Z}M_s.
\end{aligned}
\]

Empty sums are zero. Then \(W>0\) and \(\max_{s\in\mathbb Z}M_s\ge W/76\).

For the prism assertion, let \(Q\subset\mathbb R^2\) be any compact full-dimensional convex polygon with \(Q\cap\mathbb Z^2\ne\varnothing\), let \(L,M\) be positive coprime integers, and let \(h,\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\) be arbitrary. Define the original prism and its complete lattice table by

\[
\begin{aligned}
P&=\{(x,y,t)\in\mathbb R^3:(x,y)\in Q,\ 0\le t-Lx-My\le1\},\\
D&=P\cap\mathbb Z^3,\\
w_{(x,y,t)}&=\exp\bigl(-(t-h)^2+\alpha x+\beta y\bigr)
&&((x,y,t)\in D),\\
W&=\sum_{I\in D}w_I.
\end{aligned}
\]

Here and below \(W\) is the total weight of this prism table when discussing the prism. For \(k\in\mathbb Z\), define its original height mass by \(W_k=\sum_{I\in D:I_3=k}w_I\). For every \(J\in D\) with \(J_3=k\), define the true restricted depth on the singleton height band by

\[
\tau_{[k,k]}(J)=
\inf_{\substack{H\subseteq\mathbb R^3\text{ a closed halfspace}\\J\in H}}
\ \sum_{\substack{I\in D\cap H\\I_3=k}}w_I.
\]

There exist \(k_0\in\mathbb Z\) and \(J\in D\) with \(J_3=k_0\) such that simultaneously \(W_{k_0}\ge W/152\) and \(\tau_{[k_0,k_0]}(J)\ge W/304\). The band \([k_0,k_0]\) has width zero, so the same center and band are permitted by every nonnegative bound on the squared band width. All sums in these assertions retain every original lattice point, including both residual boundaries \(t-Lx-My=0,1\).
